title: Running on Empty: Early Signs, and Gentle Ways to Refill
excerpt: The quiet early signals that you're running low — and small, realistic ways to start refilling before empty.

value.text: Most of us know how to notice a full tank and an empty one. It is the long, slow slide in between that tends to go unremarked. Running on empty rarely announces itself. It creeps in as a low hum beneath an otherwise functioning life — the coffee that stops working, the weekend that no longer restores, the sense of doing everything while feeling curiously absent from it.

The good news is that the early signs are readable, if we learn to look. And catching them early matters, because refilling from low is far gentler than recovering from empty. This piece is about those quiet signals, and about small, realistic ways to start topping up before the reserves run out.
Early depletion tends to whisper rather than shout. It shows up in the texture of ordinary days more than in any single dramatic moment:

items: Rest that no longer restores — waking tired, weekends that leave you no fuller than before.
A shrinking emotional range — less delight, less spark, a flat "fine" settling over everything.
Small tasks feeling disproportionately heavy, as though everything now costs more.
Quietly withdrawing from people and activities that usually sustain you.
A body keeping the score — tension in the shoulders, shallow sleep, a stomach that tightens before the week begins.
Irritability that surprises you, arriving faster and hotter than the situation seems to warrant.

value.text: None of these are failings. They are messages from a system that has been carrying a lot for a long time, quietly asking for attention.

Part of what makes early depletion so easy to miss is how capable many people remain while it builds. You can be highly effective and quietly running low at the same time. Because you are still coping, there is never an obvious moment to stop — and the belief that you should be able to handle it keeps you pushing past the point where a pause would help. I explore this gap between coping and wellbeing more fully in this piece on [functioning well versus feeling well](/blog/functioning-well-vs-feeling-well).
The result is that the very competence that earns praise can also hide how depleted you have become — from others, and often from yourself.

Refilling does not require a retreat or a reinvented life. In fact, grand plans often collapse under their own weight. What tends to work is small, repeatable, and forgiving — little deposits made regularly rather than one heroic rescue. A few places to start:

items: Protect one genuine pause in the day — a short walk, a real lunch, ten minutes with no screen and no task.
Guard your sleep as if it mattered as much as your deadlines, because it does.
Reintroduce one small thing you enjoy for its own sake, not for its usefulness.
Practise saying no, or not yet, to protect a little of your capacity before it is all spoken for.
Move your body gently — not as another item on the list, but as a way of discharging the day.
Let some things be good enough rather than perfect, and notice that the sky stays up.

value.text: When small steps are not enough

Sometimes the tank has been low for so long that self-help alone does not quite reach it — the tiredness has roots, and the patterns feel hard to shift on your own. That is not a failure of willpower; it is simply a sign that the load has outgrown the tools you have to hand.

Counselling can offer a steady, reflective space to understand how the depletion built up and to experiment, gently, with new ways of responding to your own needs and pace. If you would like to explore what that might look like, you can read more about [burnout prevention](/work-with-me/burnout-prevention). Catching yourself while you are merely low, rather than waiting for empty, is not an overreaction. It is one of the kindest things you can do for the version of you that has to live tomorrow.
